title: Paper 2 Questions 1 and 2: true statements and the summary
specPoints: Paper 2 Section A: Question 1 (AO1, 4 marks) and Question 2 (AO1, 8 marks)

tips.title: Four, and only four
tips.body: Question 1 asks you to choose four statements which are true, and to choose a maximum of four; in June 2024 four of the eight were true. Read the lines again before deciding, because the false statements are made of words that are in them.

tips.title: Test every word
tips.body: A statement is true only if every word in it is supported by the lines: not only, not in 1998, not the thought when the passage has only the word. The added word is the one to find.

tips.title: Paraphrase is Level 1
tips.body: Restating the source shows it was read; inferring shows it was understood. Every detail in a Question 2 answer is there to support what the reader understands from it.

tips.title: Difference in the grammar
tips.body: Whereas, both … but, unlike: put the two texts in one sentence and the synthesis is done. Two paragraphs, one per source, are two summaries and a Level 3 ceiling.

tips.title: No language in Question 2
tips.body: A metaphor analysed in the summary earns nothing; it is AO2 and belongs to Question 3. If a sentence names a technique, move it.

tips.title: How, not that
tips.body: The places differ is clear; too many people in one and no people at all in the other is perceptive. Sharpen every difference into how before moving on.

why.matters: Two texts on one subject, written sixty or a hundred and sixty years apart, are the commonest way an idea reaches a reader: two reports of the same event, two accounts of the same job, two arguments about the same policy. Question 1 tests whether a reader can tell what a text actually says from what it nearly says, one word at a time; Question 2 tests whether two texts can be held together and what each lets the reader understand can be stated as a difference. Both are AO1, a tenth of the qualification, and both are the reading habits that make the comparison in Question 4 possible.

examples.title: Two accounts of the same event
examples.body: Two newspapers report the same strike, the same match, the same storm, and a reader who can say what each lets them understand, and how the accounts differ, has done Question 2. The habit of pulling the inference out of the detail, and of putting the two accounts in one sentence rather than reading them one after the other, is how anyone reads more than one source of news without being pushed about by either.

examples.title: The statement that is nearly true
examples.body: A claim in an advertisement, a line in a manifesto, a summary of a report in a headline: each is made of true words arranged so that a reader agrees before checking. Question 1's method, testing every word of a statement against the lines that are supposed to support it, is the method for reading those, and the word to look for is usually only, always or never.

steps.title: Paper 2 in one look
steps.body:
Paper 2, *Writers' viewpoints and perspectives*, is the same length and weight as Paper 1: 1 hour 45 minutes, 80 marks, half the GCSE, with the same advice of about 15 minutes reading, 45 on Section A and 45 on Section B. The difference is the insert: two non-fiction sources instead of one fiction extract, one from the 19th century and one from the 20th or 21st, linked by a theme.

**June 2024.** Source A was Adam Kay's diary of a junior doctor, published in 2017; Source B was Mary Seacole's memoir of nursing at a harbour in wartime, published in 1857. The theme was medical care, and the writing task was an article on choosing a career.

**Four reading questions, rising in size.** Question 1, 4 marks: four true statements about a few lines of Source A. Question 2, 8 marks: a summary drawing on both sources. Question 3, 12 marks: language in a passage of one source. Question 4, 16 marks: a comparison of the two writers' perspectives across both whole sources. Then Question 5, 40 marks: writing to present a viewpoint.

This topic takes the first two, both AO1: finding and interpreting information, and synthesising evidence from two texts.

Write a summary of what you understand about …
How does the writer use language to …
Compare how the writers convey their perspectives
Write an article, letter or speech
A statement, a form, an audience

steps.title: Question 1: four true statements
steps.body:
Question 1 names a few lines of Source A, prints eight statements, and asks for the four that are true. One mark each. The instructions say to choose a maximum of four, so shade four and no more.

**How the false ones are built.** From words that are in the passage, rearranged. June 2024, lines 1 to 13 of the doctor's diary: *Universities decide who to accept based only on their A-level grades* was false, and the trap was *only*. *Adam Kay finished medical school in 1998* was false, because the date in the passage was for something else. *Adam Kay thought changing his name would make him a criminal* was false: the passage had the name and the word, not the thought.

**How the true ones are built.** Often as inferences the passage supports: *The time it took for Adam Kay to become a doctor went slowly* was true, and nowhere did the passage say *slowly*; it showed it.

**The method.** Read the lines again, then test each statement against them one word at a time. A statement is true only if every word in it is supported.

The passage says schools are oversubscribed
Universities decide based only on A-level grades
The word only: candidates are interviewed
Adam Kay's musical qualifications helped him get a place
Adam Kay finished medical school in 1998
The date belongs to something else
Learning about the body was a straightforward task
Adam Kay was excited by the thought of becoming a doctor
Changing his name would make him a criminal
The words are there; the thought is not
The time it took to become a doctor went slowly

steps.title: The practice pair, one: Mary Seacole at the harbour
steps.body:
The sources in this unit are out of copyright and printed in full. The first is the 19th-century one: Mary Seacole, a Jamaican-born nurse, arriving at the harbour of Balaclava during the Crimean War in 1855 and writing about it two years later. AQA used a shortened version of this passage as its June 2024 Source B; here it is as she wrote it.

> Such a busy scene as that small harbour presented could be rarely met with elsewhere. Crowded with shipping, of every size and variety, from the noble English steamer to the smallest long-shore craft, while between them and the shore passed and repassed innumerable boats; men-of-war's boats, trim and stern; merchant-ship's boats, laden to the gunwales; Greek and Maltese boats, carrying their owners everywhere on their missions of sharp dealing and roguery. Coming from the quiet gloomy sea into this little nook of life and bustle the transition is very sudden and startling, and gives one enough to think about without desiring to go on shore this afternoon.

> I remained six weeks in Balaclava, spending my days on shore, and my nights on board ship. Over our stores, stacked on the shore, a few sheets of rough tarpaulin were suspended; and beneath these—my sole protection against the Crimean rain and wind—I spent some portion of each day, receiving visitors and selling stores.

> But my chief occupation, and one with which I never allowed any business to interfere, was helping the doctors to transfer the sick and wounded from the mules and ambulances into the transports that had to carry them to the hospitals of Scutari and Buyukdere. I did not forget the main object of my journey, to which I would have devoted myself exclusively had I been allowed; and very familiar did I become before long with the sick wharf of Balaclava. My acquaintance with it began very shortly after I had reached Balaclava. The very first day that I approached the wharf, a party of sick and wounded had just arrived. Here was work for me, I felt sure. With so many patients, the doctors must be glad of all the hands they could get. Indeed, so strong was the old impulse within me, that I waited for no permission, but seeing a poor artilleryman stretched upon a pallet, groaning heavily, I ran up to him at once, and eased the stiff dressings. Lightly my practised fingers ran over the familiar work, and well was I rewarded when the poor fellow's groans subsided into a restless uneasy mutter. God help him! He had been hit in the forehead, and I think his sight was gone. I stooped down, and raised some tea to his baked lips (here and there upon the wharf were rows of little pannikins containing this beverage). Then his hand touched mine, and rested there, and I heard him mutter indistinctly, as though the discovery had arrested his wandering senses—

Read it twice, as on Paper 1: once for what happens, once with a pencil.

rows: The harbour was crowded with shipping of every size
Seacole found the harbour quiet and gloomy
False: the sea was quiet and gloomy; the harbour was bustle
She stayed at Balaclava for six months
She spent her nights on board ship
Her chief occupation was helping to move the sick and wounded into boats
She had come to Balaclava to do nothing but this work
False: the main object of her journey was something else

steps.title: The practice pair, two: Shackleton on Elephant Island
steps.body:
The second source is 20th-century: Ernest Shackleton's *South* (1919), his account of the expedition whose ship was crushed by ice in 1915. Here, in April 1916, his men are stranded on Elephant Island and he is deciding whether to sail for help.

> A boat journey in search of relief was necessary and must not be delayed. That conclusion was forced upon me. The nearest port where assistance could certainly be secured was Port Stanley, in the Falkland Islands, 540 miles away, but we could scarcely hope to beat up against the prevailing north-westerly wind in a frail and weakened boat with a small sail area. South Georgia was over 800 miles away, but lay in the area of the west winds, and I could count upon finding whalers at any of the whaling-stations on the east coast. A boat party might make the voyage and be back with relief within a month, provided that the sea was clear of ice and the boat survive the great seas. It was not difficult to decide that South Georgia must be the objective, and I proceeded to plan ways and means. The hazards of a boat journey across 800 miles of stormy sub-Antarctic ocean were obvious, but I calculated that at worst the venture would add nothing to the risks of the men left on the island. There would be fewer mouths to feed during the winter and the boat would not require to take more than one month's provisions for six men, for if we did not make South Georgia in that time we were sure to go under. A consideration that had weight with me was that there was no chance at all of any search being made for us on Elephant Island.

The pair is linked the way AQA links its sources: two people, sixty years apart, writing about deciding to act in a place where the ordinary help is not there.

rows: The nearest port with certain help was Port Stanley, 540 miles away
Shackleton expected to find no ships at South Georgia
False: he could count on finding whalers
The boat would carry one month's provisions for six men
A search party was likely to look for them on Elephant Island
Shackleton decided that Port Stanley must be the objective

steps.title: Question 2: the summary
steps.body:
Question 2 names a focus and asks for a summary of what you understand about it from both sources. June 2024: the doctor and the nurse are working in different places; use details from both sources to write a summary of what you understand about the different places in which they are working. Eight marks, AO1, both bullets: identify and interpret, and select and synthesise from two texts.

**Four levels.** Level 4, 7 to 8, perceptive, detailed summary: perceptive inferences from both texts; judicious references relevant to the focus; statements that show perceptive differences between the texts. Level 3, 5 to 6, clear, relevant summary: clear inferences, clear references, clear differences. Level 2, 3 to 4, some attempts at summary: some inference from one or both. Level 1, 1 to 2, simple, limited: paraphrase rather than inference.

**Three words to hold.** *Inference*: what the detail lets you understand, beyond what it says. *Synthesis*: the two texts brought together in one statement of difference, not two lists. *Focus*: the thing the question names, and nothing else.

**What is not wanted.** Language analysis. A comment on a metaphor is Question 3 work and earns nothing here.

visuals.alt: A table of the four levels of Question 2 with marks and the descriptors for inference, references and difference

check.prompt: Which of these earns nothing in Question 2, however well it is done?
check.solution: Question 2 is AO1: inference, selection and synthesis. The effect of a metaphor is AO2 and belongs to Question 3; written here it is off the objective. The other three are the three bullets of the descriptor.

markScheme.description: Analysing the effect of a metaphor in one of the sources

steps.title: A Level 4 summary on the practice pair
steps.body: Focus: *the two writers are in very different situations; write a summary of what you understand about the situations they face.* Here is one paragraph built to the descriptors, on Seacole and Shackleton.

visuals.problem: Write a Level 4 summary of the different situations the two writers face.

steps.text: A statement of difference first: Seacole has arrived at a place overflowing with people and help, Shackleton at one where help has to be fetched across 800 miles of sea.
steps.note: Both texts in one sentence, on the focus: that is synthesis.

steps.text: Detail and inference from Source A: the harbour is “Crowded with shipping, of every size and variety”, with boats passing and repassing between ships and shore, which suggests a place where the war's whole supply and rescue is funnelled through one small basin.
steps.note: A judicious detail, then what it lets the reader understand.

steps.text: Detail and inference from Source B: the nearest certain help is Port Stanley, “540 miles away”, and the chosen goal is further still, from which the reader understands that the men are beyond any help that does not come from themselves.
steps.note: The same move on the other text.

steps.text: A second difference, sharpened: Seacole's difficulty is that there are too many wounded for the hands available; Shackleton's is that “there was no chance at all of any search being made for us on Elephant Island”.
steps.note: A perceptive difference: not that the places differ, but how the danger differs.

steps.text: A closing inference across both: both writers respond by acting without waiting to be asked or rescued, but Seacole steps into a crowd and Shackleton steps out of one.
steps.note: Perceptive, and still on the focus. No language analysis anywhere.

rows: Synthesis: both texts in one sentence
The same on the other text

check.solution: Inference is understanding beyond what is stated; synthesis is the two texts in one statement. The sentence does both and stays on the focus. A shorter restatement of the passages would be paraphrase, which is the Level 1 word.

steps.title: Eight statements, four true
steps.body:
Write eight statements about the first paragraph of the Seacole passage, exactly four of them true, in the style of the paper: build the false ones from words that are in the passage, with one word added or shifted. Then swap with someone, or come back tomorrow, and answer your own.

Then a summary in five sentences on this focus: *what you understand about how the two writers see the people around them*. Both texts in the first sentence; a detail and an inference from each; a difference that says how, not just that.

steps.title: Perceptive: inference and difference
steps.body:
The Level 4 words for Question 2 are perceptive inferences, judicious references and perceptive differences. Three habits produce them.

**Infer, do not list.** A list of details from each source is Level 1 or 2 however long. Each detail is there to support what the reader understands: *rows of little metal cups* is a detail; that the wharf had been organised to give the wounded tea while they waited is an inference.

**Synthesise in the sentence.** *Whereas*, *both … but*, *unlike*: the difference lives in the grammar. Two paragraphs, one per source, are two summaries.

**Say how, not just that.** The places differ is Level 3; the danger in one is too many people and in the other no people at all is Level 4. The June 2024 Level 4 example did exactly this: both places chaotic, but one a safe hospital in peacetime and the other a warzone without shelter or beds.

**And keep to eight marks' worth of time:** ten minutes, no language analysis, and on to the twelve marks of Question 3.

steps.title: Questions 1 and 2 in one page
steps.body:
Twelve marks, about fifteen minutes, both AO1.

- **The paper:** two non-fiction sources, 19th century and 20th or 21st, linked by a theme; 15 minutes reading; Questions 1 to 4 rise from 4 to 16 marks.
- **Question 1, 4 marks:** eight statements; choose the four that are true, and a maximum of four; test every word against the lines; the false ones are the passage's words with something added or shifted.
- **Question 2, 8 marks:** a summary on the named focus from both sources; inference, not paraphrase; synthesis, not two lists; the difference sharpened into how.
- **No language analysis in either.** That is Question 3.
- **The practice pair:** Seacole at the harbour, 1857; Shackleton on Elephant Island, 1919; both public domain, both printed in full.

Question 3 and Question 4 have their own topics, and the 19th-century source has a topic of its own.

A list; two paragraphs; a metaphor analysed

questions.prompt:
**Seacole passage.**

> Such a busy scene as that small harbour presented could be rarely met with elsewhere. Crowded with shipping, of every size and variety, from the noble English steamer to the smallest long-shore craft, while between them and the shore passed and repassed innumerable boats; men-of-war's boats, trim and stern; merchant-ship's boats, laden to the gunwales; Greek and Maltese boats, carrying their owners everywhere on their missions of sharp dealing and roguery. Coming from the quiet gloomy sea into this little nook of life and bustle the transition is very sudden and startling, and gives one enough to think about without desiring to go on shore this afternoon.

> I remained six weeks in Balaclava, spending my days on shore, and my nights on board ship. Over our stores, stacked on the shore, a few sheets of rough tarpaulin were suspended; and beneath these—my sole protection against the Crimean rain and wind—I spent some portion of each day, receiving visitors and selling stores.

> But my chief occupation, and one with which I never allowed any business to interfere, was helping the doctors to transfer the sick and wounded from the mules and ambulances into the transports that had to carry them to the hospitals of Scutari and Buyukdere. I did not forget the main object of my journey, to which I would have devoted myself exclusively had I been allowed; and very familiar did I become before long with the sick wharf of Balaclava. My acquaintance with it began very shortly after I had reached Balaclava. The very first day that I approached the wharf, a party of sick and wounded had just arrived. Here was work for me, I felt sure. With so many patients, the doctors must be glad of all the hands they could get. Indeed, so strong was the old impulse within me, that I waited for no permission, but seeing a poor artilleryman stretched upon a pallet, groaning heavily, I ran up to him at once, and eased the stiff dressings. Lightly my practised fingers ran over the familiar work, and well was I rewarded when the poor fellow's groans subsided into a restless uneasy mutter. God help him! He had been hit in the forehead, and I think his sight was gone. I stooped down, and raised some tea to his baked lips (here and there upon the wharf were rows of little pannikins containing this beverage). Then his hand touched mine, and rested there, and I heard him mutter indistinctly, as though the discovery had arrested his wandering senses—

**Shackleton passage.**

> A boat journey in search of relief was necessary and must not be delayed. That conclusion was forced upon me. The nearest port where assistance could certainly be secured was Port Stanley, in the Falkland Islands, 540 miles away, but we could scarcely hope to beat up against the prevailing north-westerly wind in a frail and weakened boat with a small sail area. South Georgia was over 800 miles away, but lay in the area of the west winds, and I could count upon finding whalers at any of the whaling-stations on the east coast. A boat party might make the voyage and be back with relief within a month, provided that the sea was clear of ice and the boat survive the great seas. It was not difficult to decide that South Georgia must be the objective, and I proceeded to plan ways and means. The hazards of a boat journey across 800 miles of stormy sub-Antarctic ocean were obvious, but I calculated that at worst the venture would add nothing to the risks of the men left on the island. There would be fewer mouths to feed during the winter and the boat would not require to take more than one month's provisions for six men, for if we did not make South Georgia in that time we were sure to go under. A consideration that had weight with me was that there was no chance at all of any search being made for us on Elephant Island.

Both writers face situations in which the ordinary help is not there. Use details from both practice sources to write a summary of what you understand about the situations they face. Aim for the length you would write for eight marks, about ten minutes.
questions.solution: Both writers face a place beyond the ordinary reach of help, but the shape of the difficulty is opposite in each. Seacole arrives at a harbour “Crowded with shipping, of every size and variety”, with boats passing and repassing between the ships and the shore, from which the reader understands that the war's whole traffic of supply and rescue is being funnelled through one small basin, and that the problem there is too much to do rather than nothing to be done. Her chief occupation, helping to move the sick and wounded from the ambulances into the boats, suggests a system that exists but is overwhelmed, short of hands rather than of will. Shackleton's situation is the reverse. The nearest port where help could certainly be found is “540 miles away” and the goal he chooses is further still, and he states plainly that “there was no chance at all of any search being made for us on Elephant Island”; the reader understands that no system reaches him, and that the only help will be the help he fetches himself across an ocean he calls the most tempestuous in the world. Both respond by acting without waiting for permission or rescue, but Seacole steps into a crowd of helpers and Shackleton steps out of the only company he has.

F: reversed sense, the north-westerly wind was against it. C. South Georgia was over 800 miles away. T. D. examTechnique.body:
**Two sources, one theme, fifteen minutes' reading.** Both texts twice, then all five questions, before writing.

**Question 1, 4 marks, about four minutes.** Read the named lines again. Test every word of each statement. Choose the four that are true, and a maximum of four.

**Question 2, 8 marks, about ten minutes.** The named focus only. Both texts in the first sentence. A detail and an inference from each. The difference sharpened into how. No language analysis.

**Then move on.** Question 3 is twelve marks and Question 4 sixteen; the summary is not where the paper is won.
examinerErrors: Shading more than four statements in Question 1, against the instruction to choose a maximum of four.
Treating a statement as true because its words are in the passage, when one word has been added or reversed.
Writing a summary of one source and then a summary of the other, so nothing is synthesised.
Paraphrasing the sources instead of inferring from them, which is the Level 1 wording.
Analysing language in Question 2, which is AO2 and earns nothing on an AO1 question.
Spending twenty minutes on eight marks and running short for Question 4 and the writing.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer to Question 1 is four shaded circles, each checked word by word against the lines, done in four minutes. To Question 2 it is a short paragraph that begins with both texts in one statement of difference on the named focus, gives a judicious detail from each source with the inference it supports, sharpens the difference into how rather than that, and stops. It infers rather than paraphrases, synthesises rather than lists, never analyses language, and leaves the time the bigger questions need.
